This situation underscores the need for a public discussion about the intersection of health services and education. 🦠 DID NATURAL CHICKENPOX HAVE AN UNEXPECTED IMMUNE BENEFIT?

For generations, chickenpox was an almost universal childhood infection. Then, beginning in the mid-1990s, routine childhood vaccination dramatically reduced natural chickenpox.

That was intended to prevent chickenpox and its complications.

But could eliminating widespread natural infection—and repeated exposure to it—also have changed our immune environment in ways we didn’t fully anticipate?

There are two intriguing areas of research.

1️⃣ Chickenpox exposure and shingles

After recovering from chickenpox, varicella-zoster virus remains dormant in the body and can later reactivate as shingles.

Researchers have found evidence for something called “exogenous immune boosting.” Adults who were periodically exposed to children with natural chickenpox appeared to receive an immune-system “reminder” that strengthened their VZV immunity.

One large study found adults living with a child who developed chickenpox had about a 33% lower incidence of shingles during the following two years.

As childhood chickenpox became uncommon, those repeated natural exposures largely disappeared.

Does that help explain some of the long-term changes we’ve seen in shingles?

Possibly.

2️⃣ Chickenpox and glioma

This one particularly caught my attention because some of the early research was conducted right here in the San Francisco Bay Area.

Researchers repeatedly found an intriguing association between previous chickenpox/VZV immunity and a lower likelihood of adult glioma, including glioblastoma.

A 2005 Bay Area study found people reporting previous chickenpox had about 41% lower odds of glioma, and higher VZV antibody levels were also associated with lower odds.

A much larger international study later found a smaller but still significant association—about 21% lower odds of glioma among people reporting previous chickenpox.

That does NOT mean chickenpox has been proven to prevent brain cancer. Association is not causation.

But it raises an important scientific question:

Could natural childhood infections sometimes produce long-term immune effects that extend far beyond protection against the original illness?

Medicine should be willing to investigate both sides of that question.

When we fundamentally alter the way a population encounters a virus that co-evolved with humans for thousands of years, we should also study the downstream effects—beneficial, harmful and unexpected.

Science isn’t served by assuming the answer.

It represents one of the most comprehensive evaluations of nattokinase to date, uniquely integrating its proteolytic, cardiovascular, pharmacokinetic, amyloid, and spike-protein literature into a single review.

SPIKE PROTEIN DEGRADATION

Different preparations, different model systems, same basic conclusion: spike protein is susceptible to degradation by this class of proteolytic enzymes.

AMYLOID DEGRADATION

Nattokinase has also demonstrated activity against several structurally distinct amyloid proteins.

Published studies report degradation of Aβ40, Aβ42, human prion peptide fibrils, insulin fibrils, and β2-microglobulin fibrils. This broad activity suggests that nattokinase can attack abnormal cross-β protein structures rather than acting on only one specific amyloid protein.

AMYLOID MICROCLOT DISSOLUTION

BOOSTING THE BODY’S NATURAL CLOT-DISSOLVING SYSTEM

September 24, 2026

A senior at a New York high school can no longer attend class as of today, after a federal judge declined to extend a medical exemption from the school’s vaccine mandates for the current school year.

Last year, U.S. District Judge Gary Brown of the Eastern District of New York ordered a New York school district to allow Sarah Doe, who had obtained a medical exemption, to attend high school during the 2025-2026 school year.

But in a ruling issued late Wednesday in Jane Doe v. Oceanside Union Free School District, Brown denied the renewed medical exemption request for the 2026-2027 school year.

Last year, Brown granted an emergency preliminary injunction allowing Sarah to attend 11th grade without receiving the third dose of the hepatitis B (Hep B) vaccine — the only recommended shot she hadn’t taken at the time — because her severe reactions to previous doses had left her sick and disabled.

When the lawsuit was filed, at least six treating physicians certified to the school district that Sarah could be harmed by taking the shot, according to court documents. The district nonetheless repeatedly denied her exemption requests. Since then, more doctors have affirmed that assessment.

Brown said last year’s decision rested in part on a physician’s report that Sarah experienced an anaphylactic reaction to an earlier dose, and evidence she had received the first two doses and had some immunity.

Brown also based his previous decision on an appeals court precedent stating that there had never been definitive proof that hepatitis B could be transmitted through “non-parenteral” routes like saliva — meaning passed in ways not transmitted through blood or broken skin.

After attending school last year under the court order, Sarah applied for a medical exemption from the Hep B vaccine and also the second meningococcal vaccine required for this school year.

The school district again denied her request. Sarah’s lawyers responded by filing an emergency motion seeking a new court order allowing her to return to school this year.

Explaining his latest decision, Brown said this year’s circumstances were “substantially different.” This year, Sarah would be attending school without two of the mandated vaccines, instead of one. And, he said, there was insufficient medical evidence showing that she could not receive the meningococcal vaccine.

“At the end of the day, Sarah is a child who just wants to go to school,” her attorney, Sujata Gibson, told The Defender.

Gibson said:

“Nine doctors and specialists have said she needs to defer vaccination. If that still isn’t enough for her to receive an accommodation, then we have to ask what protections medically fragile children actually have in New York.

“Federal disability laws are supposed to protect children like Sarah. We believe that protection failed here, and we intend to seek immediate appellate review.”

➡️This INTERESTING and small Swedish study compared 23 people with post-COVID condition (PCC, laboratory-confirmed SARSCoV2, persistent symptoms >3 months, mean ~32 months later, mostly mild/non-hospitalized) against 19 matched controls.

➡️PCC participants reported far higher visual symptoms (reading difficulty, light sensitivity, intolerance of busy visual environments, motion sensitivity) plus general and mental fatigue.

➡️Objective visual function was mostly preserved.

➡️The main deficits appeared in dynamic measures: reduced vergence facility among those with high near-vision symptom scores, and slower Developmental Eye Movement test times.

➡️Optical coherence tomography showed no significant thinning of retinal nerve fibre layer (RNFL) or ganglion cell layer.

➡️However, normal correlations between RNFL and ganglion-cell complex were disrupted in the PCC group. Lower RNFL thickness correlated with worse executive function (Stroop) and poorer vergence facility.

➡️Cognition showed slower psychomotor processing speed and a trend toward weaker executive function.

➡️The picture is one of prominent subjective visual and fatigue complaints with only subtle, interconnected objective signals rather than frank structural damage.

1. I received measles vaccines as a child. Am I still protected?

For most people, yes. Two doses of MMR given on or after the first birthday, at least 28 days apart, are about 97% effective against measles and are considered lifelong protection. One dose is about 93% effective and is enough for most adults who are not in higher-risk settings. Immunity from the live vaccine is generally long-term. Rare breakthrough infections can still happen, but they are uncommon.

2. What should I do if I cannot find my vaccination records?

First try to locate records (old shot cards, school or military records, or your doctor’s office). If you cannot find them and you do not have other evidence of immunity, talk with a clinician. Many adults can simply receive a dose of MMR. There is no harm in an extra dose if you are already immune. People born before 1957 are generally presumed immune from natural infection.

4. Does pregnancy, chemotherapy, or another health condition change what I should do?

Yes. MMR is a live vaccine and is contraindicated in pregnancy and in some people with severely weakened immune systems. People who are pregnant, planning pregnancy, or immunocompromised (for example, certain chemotherapy or other immunosuppressive treatment) should discuss measles risk and options with their clinician rather than getting MMR on their own. Close contacts who are eligible can still be vaccinated to reduce household risk. Adults over 20, pregnant people, and those with weakened immunity also have a higher risk of measles complications if they become infected.

3. Do I need a titer test or another MMR dose?

Not routinely. CDC accepts written proof of adequate vaccination, a positive measles IgG test, lab-confirmed past measles, or birth before 1957 as evidence of immunity. Serologic testing is optional, not required before vaccination. Documented vaccination usually takes precedence over a later titer result. Extra MMR doses are not recommended as a catch-up program for the general adult population. High-risk adults (healthcare workers, international travelers, students in post-high-school settings) often need two documented doses.

The agency has lost its independence and nearly a third of its staff, as Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and associates have tightened control.

For decades, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention was the undisputed global leader in public health. Its scientists helped train health officials worldwide. In the United States, it was the primary source of guidance for prevention and treatment of diseases, including diabetes, H.I.V. and the seasonal flu.

But after a year and a half in the cross hairs of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s drive to remake public health policy, the agency is a skeleton of the powerhouse it was.

The Trump administration’s widespread layoffs in early 2025 cut 18 percent of the C.D.C.’s staff. But new personnel data, compiled by a group of former federal scientists and reported here for the first time, indicate that the agency’s staff has dwindled far more, as large numbers of employees retired or resigned. As of May 2026, the C.D.C. had 30 percent fewer employees than it did before the layoffs, the data show.

Interviews with more than 30 current and former employees reveal the agency is now tightly controlled by Mr. Kennedy and his associates, and its scientists are finding it increasingly difficult to do their jobs effectively. (Some of them spoke on the condition of anonymity because of a fear of retaliation from the administration.)

The number of C.D.C. employees has fallen sharply in one year

The changes have hindered the C.D.C.’s ability to respond to outbreaks as measles spreads at home and Ebola abroad, and to issue timely guidance on vaccinations as cooling temperatures kick off the respiratory season, according to current and former employees. State and local health departments, which rely on the C.D.C. for resources and technical advice, have been stymied by delays. Entire divisions have been shuttered, including teams that worked on smoking, sexual violence, child abuse and falls among older adults.

Even some areas central to the Trump administration’s priorities have been gutted. Despite Mr. Kennedy’s focus on chronic diseases and autism, the C.D.C. centers that aim to prevent chronic diseases and birth defects are at half their previous size, according to the new data, compiled by the Public Data Observatory from the Office of Personnel Management, the Department of Health and Human Services, and the employee union.

The layoffs spared the agency’s infectious disease centers. But even so, the center for emerging and zoonotic diseases, which manages Ebola and hantavirus, among others, now has nearly 300 fewer employees than in March 2025, and the respiratory disease center has lost nearly 200 — about 17 percent in each case.

Beyond staff reductions, there is a leadership vacuum. Only one of the 11 center directors from March 2025 remains at the agency. Most of the other centers are being run by acting directors, some of whom were elevated from jobs one or two levels below.

“It’s a zombified C.D.C. where you have all the bits and pieces — like the body’s there, the substance is there, but it’s not acting like how an agency like that should act,” said Dr. Demetre Daskalakis, who led the respiratory disease center before he resigned in August 2025.

Despite a series of high-profile disease outbreaks, C.D.C. workers have had little contact with the World Health Organization, with members of Congress and even, for a time, with their partners in state and local health departments, some employees said. Statements to the media about health crises are also tightly controlled by H.H.S.

Even basic functions have broken down. Travel approvals take months; upkeep of bathrooms and vacuuming of offices have been disrupted, some current employees said.

One senior official said it felt as though the agency was being held together with bubble gum and duct tape, with employees running from crisis to crisis, and nothing working the way it is supposed to.

The Department of Health and Human Services did not respond to a series of questions about the C.D.C.’s work, staffing and independence. “C.D.C. continues to protect the health and safety of the American people and communicate clearly about the importance of vaccination,” the department said in an emailed statement.

But several former officials disagreed with that assessment, noting that the C.D.C. has offered little leadership or clear communication even as, in just a few months, the nation has grappled with record cases of measles, cyclosporiasis and rabies.
“Imagine losing a third of a city’s firefighters and then wondering why downtown is burning,” said Dr. Jonathan Mermin, who led the agency’s center for H.I.V. and sexually transmitted infections till April 2025, and is now the dean of the Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health.

Political Interference
From the very first day of Mr. Trump’s second term, when he withdrew the country from the W.H.O., his administration has sought to upend the nation’s health policies and align them with his political priorities.

In past administrations, just two or three political appointees had purview over the C.D.C. Now, there are nearly 20 political appointees from H.H.S. who communicate with C.D.C. staff members, sometimes directing them to spend time and funding on dubious theories outside the agency’s scope, according to several officials.

Last year, an H.H.S. official directed the C.D.C. to award a no-bid contract — a rarity for the agency — to Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute to explore whether immunizing pregnant women would lead to autism in their children, a theory that Mr. Kennedy has espoused but that has been debunked by numerous studies. To pay for the research, the C.D.C. took $362,000 from a program that provides free vaccines to about half of American children.

In an email viewed by The New York Times, Stuart Burns, a political appointee, asked C.D.C. employees to pull together details of every measles case since 2010, including patients’ underlying medical conditions with diagnostic codes; that information is not collected routinely, they told him. Mr. Kennedy has falsely argued that measles only causes death in children who are already ill with other conditions.

Dr. William “Reyn” Archer III, another appointee who previously oversaw the C.D.C., repeatedly asked agency employees to work on screwworm, a disease that mostly affects cattle, even though the C.D.C.’s mission is to protect human health, said Dr. Daniel Jernigan, who headed the agency’s emerging disease center before resigning in August 2025. Dr. Archer did not respond to a request for comment.

Mr. Kennedy’s associates outside the administration have also been allowed direct access to senior C.D.C. staff members. Dr. Ben Edwards, a physician in Lubbock, Texas, who treated children while he was infected with measles and whom Mr. Kennedy had praised as an “extraordinary” healer, asked senior C.D.C. officials to look into cod liver oil as a treatment for measles, citing “historical references dating back to the 1700s,” in an email viewed by The Times.

“We just would have to run around constantly to be responsive to all of these strange asks,” recalled Dr. Daskalakis, the former head of the respiratory disease center.

Numerous other instances of political interference in the C.D.C.’s activities have already been reported. Most notably, Mr. Kennedy openly overruled the C.D.C.’s scientists in imposing strict quarantine measures for people exposed to hantavirus. Dr. Jay Bhattacharya, who led the agency for six months in the absence of a Senate-confirmed director, squashed publication of a study on the effectiveness of Covid vaccines.

Some observers had hoped the C.D.C.’s new director, Dr. Erica Schwartz, a physician who has pledged to “follow the science,” would provide a bulwark against political interference. Delays and Dysfunction
Across the C.D.C., the employees who remain are backfilling roles left vacant.

“I’ve never seen such a plethora of acting roles in my life,” the agency’s new chief operating officer, Sean Slovenski, acknowledged to staff members at a meeting in June, a recording of which was obtained by The Times.

Many divisions are struggling to disburse money appropriated by Congress. In an email in May viewed by The Times, an official asked for volunteers from other offices to help the Division of Population Health, which had lost 88 percent of its staff, write notices of funding opportunities for diseases like lupus and epilepsy.

“We are overseeing millions of dollars in funded work, but how can we do this in a responsible way when we just don’t have enough people to really oversee the work well?” said one official at the agency’s chronic disease center.
The agency’s dysfunction is alarming public health experts even outside the country, who had long relied on the C.D.C.’s expertise during global crises. At a recent meeting of global flu experts, Dr. Jernigan said, “people truly believe that we are less prepared now and less capable of having a coordinated response than we were before the pandemic.”

By this time of year in 2024, the C.D.C. had published detailed recommendations for vaccines against respiratory diseases, with endorsements from the director at the time, Dr. Mandy Cohen, and notes from a meeting of its vaccine advisers.

The C.D.C.’s public health infrastructure grant, which helps health departments train employees and build systems, was managed by 20 project officers but it now has just three. As a result, the team’s response time for requests from local departments has increased from less than a day to more than 10, and some requests have been missed entirely. One county health department requested help on Aug. 7 with submitting data for its annual report but as of Sept. 21, the request was unanswered.

“We’re seeing a movement away from clinical guidance, from data, and from working with states,” said Dr. Debra Houry, who was the agency’s chief medical officer before resigning in August 2025.
In all, more than 1,200 people retired between March 2025 and May 2026, nearly four times the number in the comparable period in 2023-24. About 270 people are still on administrative leave, being paid but not working, while a lawsuit challenging the layoffs makes its way through the courts.

Hepatitis A: Causes, Symptoms, Treatment and Prevention

Hepatitis A is a contagious viral infection that affects the liver. It is caused by the hepatitis A virus (HAV) and usually causes a temporary illness. Unlike hepatitis B and C, it generally does not lead to chronic liver disease.

Causes and Spread

Hepatitis A mainly spreads through the fecal-oral route, usually when contaminated food or water is consumed. Close contact with an infected person can also transmit the virus, especially where sanitation and hand hygiene are poor.

Symptoms

Some people, particularly young children, may have few or no symptoms. Possible symptoms include:

- Fatigue and weakness
- Loss of appetite
- Nausea or vomiting
- Mild fever
- Abdominal discomfort
- Dark urine
- Pale stools
- Yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice)

Diagnosis

Doctors usually confirm hepatitis A with a blood test that detects antibodies linked to recent HAV infection. Liver function tests may also be performed to assess liver health.

Treatment

There is no specific antiviral cure for hepatitis A. Most people recover with supportive care, including adequate rest, fluids, and nutritious food. Medicines should be used according to medical advice, as some can affect the liver.

Prevention

GENITAL WARTS & HPV: WHAT EVERY MAN AND WOMAN SHOULD KNOW

Human papillomavirus (HPV) is one of the most common sexually transmitted infections. It spreads mainly through intimate skin-to-skin contact, including vaginal, anal, and oral sex.

While most HPV infections clear naturally, some types cause genital warts, while others can lead to certain cancers.

What are genital warts?
Genital warts are non-cancerous growths caused mainly by HPV types 6 and 11. They may appear as small, flesh-coloured bumps, flat growths, or clusters resembling a cauliflower.

They can be painless or cause itching, irritation, discomfort, or bleeding.

Where do genital warts appear?
In men:
Penis, including the shaft and head.
Scrotum and groin.
Around or inside the anus.

In women:
Vulva and labia.
Vaginal opening and inside the vagina.
Cervix.
Around or inside the anus.

Note: Some people have HPV without visible warts or other symptoms.

How does HPV spread?
HPV spreads through intimate skin-to-skin contact, even without penetration or visible symptoms. Condoms reduce the risk but do not provide complete protection.

HPV can remain undetected for months or years, so a diagnosis does not establish when the infection was acquired.

Can genital warts be treated?
Yes. Treatment may include prescription creams, freezing (cryotherapy), or medical removal. However, treating visible warts does not necessarily eliminate HPV from the body, and warts may return.

Never use ordinary wart-removal products or home remedies on genital skin.

Can HPV cause cancer?
Yes. Certain high-risk HPV types can cause cervical, penile, anal, vulvar, vaginal, and some throat cancers.

The HPV types that cause genital warts are generally different from those that cause cancer.

Women and others with a cervix should follow recommended cervical cancer screening guidelines.

How can you protect yourself?
Get vaccinated against HPV. The vaccine helps prevent HPV infections that cause genital warts and several cancers.
Use condoms to reduce the risk of transmission.
Get routine cervical cancer screening. 
Avoid self-medication and seek medical attention for unusual genital growths.
If diagnosed with genital warts, discuss treatment and partner communication with a healthcare professional.

When should you see a doctor?
Seek medical advice if you notice unusual genital bumps, persistent itching, sores, unexplained bleeding, or growths that are painful or changing.

A medical examination can help distinguish genital warts from other conditions.

HPV affects both men and women, and many people carry it without knowing. Having HPV or genital warts is not a reason for shame.

Get informed, get vaccinated if eligible, practice safer sex, and seek medical attention when you notice unusual changes. Early awareness and prevention can protect your health and reduce the risk of complications.

Yes. Most large immunization programs collect and report recipient data by sex (and sometimes gender identity).
What is collected
•National immunization information systems typically record biological sex as a core field. In the United States this is a standard element in Immunization Information Systems so records can be matched, forecasts can follow sex-specific schedules (for example HPV), and coverage can be analyzed by sex.17
•Some countries have added non-binary options. Australia’s Immunization Register now accepts “Gender X.”15
•COVID-19 programs published dedicated age-and-sex dashboards. CDC released national and state-level files showing first doses, completed series, and boosters by sex.1
What the data typically show
•Childhood routine vaccines: globally, boys and girls usually have similar coverage. Differences appear in some settings with strong son preference or access barriers.33
•COVID-19 (early rollout): in the United States the first weeks were 63 % female / 37 % male, largely because health-care workers and nursing-home residents were prioritized and both groups are majority female. The gap later narrowed.0
•HPV: many programs still vaccinate more girls than boys because the original target was cervical-cancer prevention; an increasing number of countries now run gender-neutral programs, but coverage among boys remains lower in most places.29
Distribution policy vs. tracking Doses themselves are generally allocated by age group, occupation, risk, or geography rather than by gender. Sex-disaggregated reporting is used afterward to detect inequities and adjust outreach. WHO and Gavi treat sex-disaggregated immunization data as a standard equity indicator.28
In short, gender/sex identification of vaccine recipients is routine in surveillance systems even though the vaccines themselves are not usually rationed by gender.

“Perfect.”

“Good.”

“Wonderful.”

His friend asked:

“What's wrong?”

“Of course.”

“Bro, the goal of healthy living isn't to become immortal.”

He sat back down.

“So what's the goal?”

 “To give yourself a better chance of living longer and healthier—and to improve the quality of the years you have.”

That answer changed the whole conversation.

Because sometimes we misunderstand health.

We think:

Eat healthy = no disease.

Exercise = no sickness.

Condom = no STI.

Drink water = perfect kidney.

No alcohol = immortal.

But life doesn't work like that.

Healthy habits reduce risks; they don't create a guarantee against death.

For example, condoms used correctly and consistently are highly effective against many STIs and HIV, but they don't eliminate every STI risk. Regular testing and appropriate vaccination also matter. 

And having one partner is not simply about saying, “I trust my partner.”

It's also about mutual testing, honesty and shared responsibility. Some STIs have no symptoms, so someone can have an infection without knowing it. 

Vaccines can prevent certain serious infections, including HPV and hepatitis B. 

Physical activity, avoiding tobacco, eating a balanced diet and avoiding alcohol are all recognized as healthy lifestyle choices. 

But here's the part people sometimes forget:

Healthy living is not a contract with God saying, “I will never die.”

It's a commitment that says:

“While I am alive, I will take care of this body and this life as much as I reasonably can.”

So yes…

Eat your vegetables.

Exercise.

Sleep properly.

Don't smoke.

Avoid excessive alcohol.

Take recommended vaccines.

Get appropriate health checks.

Practice safer sex.

Drink water according to your body's needs.

Eat a balanced diet.

Maintain good hygiene.

And please don't turn one particular food—like noodles—into the villain of your entire existence. 😂

The bigger picture is overall dietary quality, balance, moderation and variety, not simply banning one food. 

❤️ And there's an even deeper lesson.

We spend so much time trying to extend life that sometimes we forget to live it.

Call your mother.

Visit your father.

Play with your children.

Laugh with your friends.

Build something meaningful.

Help somebody.

Learn something.

Pray.

Love people.

Forgive where you can.

Take care of your body.

Take care of your mind.

And don't postpone your entire life until you become “successful.”

Because nobody was promised forever.

The point isn't to live forever.

The point is to make the life you have count.

People start saying they want to experience Bali too.

Where we move mountains without forgetting life is more than the work you do.

We are JUST getting started.

A new global analysis estimates that infections were responsible for about 2.3 million new cancer cases in 2024 — roughly 12% of all cancers diagnosed worldwide.

Remarkably, five pathogens accounted for nearly all of these infection-related cancers: Helicobacter pylori, human papillomavirus (HPV), hepatitis B virus (HBV), Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) and hepatitis C virus (HCV).

H. pylori alone was linked to around 760,000 cancer cases, mostly stomach cancer. The bacterium is extremely common — roughly half of the world’s population carries it — although most infected people never develop cancer.

HPV was linked to another 750,000 cases. Persistent infection with high-risk HPV types can cause cervical cancer as well as cancers of the throat, anus, penis, vulva and vagina. Vaccination can prevent infections responsible for many of these cancers.

Chronic hepatitis B and C infections can damage the liver over decades and increase the risk of liver cancer. EBV, which infects most humans at some point in their lives, is associated with several cancers including nasopharyngeal carcinoma and certain lymphomas.

The important part is that infection-related cancer is not inevitable. HPV and hepatitis B vaccines, hepatitis C treatment, H. pylori detection and treatment, screening and other public-health measures can prevent a significant number of cases.

About three-quarters of infection-related cancers occurred in low- and middle-income countries, showing how access to vaccination, testing and treatment can directly influence the global cancer burden.
